practice.title: Rejoicing in the Bodhisattva Paths and Grounds
agreedSteps: Rejoice in the Bodhisattva's realizations of emptiness — imagine and appreciate the ten spiritual grounds, the direct realization of emptiness, or any stage of the path. Even developing doubts about emptiness starts to destroy our samsara.
Push the boundary of what we think is possible for ourselves — identify where we've set a limit and try to expand it through rejoicing in the paths, imagining what these realizations would be like.

Practice seeing the people around us — really noticing them as a step toward rejoicing. In busy places it's easy to see people as scenery; try to see each person as important, which is the ground from which positive minds develop.
steps: Try self-generation practice at different levels of the Mahayana path — for example, imagine having spontaneous bodhichitta (path of accumulation), or tranquil abiding on emptiness where all dualistic appearances have subsided (path of preparation). What would that be like?

Stay on the cutting edge of the mind rather than retreating to safe, familiar territory. If we're genuinely engaged with what we're learning, every person we meet and every situation we encounter connects to it — a kind of Cambrian explosion of insights.

Be suspicious of the appearances in our life — they could be emanations helping us. Since countless holy beings are emanating, and we obviously have connections to at least some of them, their emanations may appear as ordinary things in our lives.

commentary.title: Rejoicing Purified by Bodhichitta
content: If we rejoice in the mind of bodhichitta, there's no way it won't be pure. We can acquire knowledge greedily, in a way that stops us from moving forward. But rejoicing done with bodhichitta naturally stays clean.

Rejoicing in others and contemplating the kindness of others are related practices — both involve contemplating the good qualities of others. If we are competitive with someone, it's hard to rejoice in them. Competitiveness often comes from thinking we are self-made. There is no competition if we realize we deserve no credit for who we are in this life.

Our self-interest can actually get us in the door — thinking that we will gain the good qualities we're rejoicing in helps motivate us, like reading the biographies of great practitioners and being inspired to emulate them.

commentary.title: Buddha Nature and Self-Generation
content: Our good qualities are our Buddha Nature, our Buddha potential. If we are kind to people, that's a sign of our Buddha Nature — a sign that we will become a fully enlightened being someday. Self-generation practice simply puts the name 'I' onto a Buddha's body and mind. Imputing 'I' onto a Buddha's body and mind and never stopping that — that's when you are a Buddha.

When we do self-generation practice enough, we feel it is our real world, so we're very happy in our heart. It doesn't matter where we are externally. Then we decide where to go and what to do based on what is most beneficial to others.

commentary.title: The Energy Knob
content: We can be virtuous in a very relaxed way. Put ninety percent of attention on our inner state, ten percent on external states, and we can stay relaxed and take care of things happily.

Most people have dialed the energy knob way up, further than they need to get things done. The experiment is: can I turn the energy knob down and still get it done? Including meditating. All that extra energy can just excite the mind. Turn the knob up and down. What's the minimum energy needed to get it done?

commentary.title: The Five Mahayana Paths
content: The five Mahayana paths are: accumulation, preparation, seeing, meditation, and no more learning (APSMAL). We enter the path of accumulation when we generate spontaneous bodhichitta — every moment of every day, bodhichitta is there without effort, the way self-grasping is spontaneous right now.

The path of preparation begins when we have tranquil abiding on emptiness. It's still conceptual — like looking through a window made of ice. As we meditate more, the ice melts, until we see emptiness directly, without a concept. That's the path of seeing.

On the path of seeing we abandon all intellectually-formed self-grasping — all the weird ideas about the world that come from bad reasoning. From a realized being's perspective, ordinary people sound completely crazy because of how many layers of confusion we talk about as if they're facts. But realized beings don't laugh at us — they have too much compassion.

From the path of seeing through the path of meditation, we progress through the ten Mahayana grounds, eroding the nine levels of innate self-grasping from big-big down to small-small. By the eighth ground, all delusions are gone. But the imprints remain — the garlic smell — and these are removed through the eighth, ninth, and tenth grounds until the Vajra-like concentration of the path of meditation, which is the last moment of the mind of a sentient being. In the next moment, the Bodhisattva becomes a Buddha.

commentary.title: The Twelve Special Qualities and Emanations
content: On the first ground, Very Joyful, a Bodhisattva can see a hundred Buddhas in one short instant, remain alive for a hundred eons, see the ends of the previous and next hundred eons, enter a hundred concentrations, cause a hundred worlds to shake, illuminate a hundred realms, ripen a hundred living beings, visit a hundred Buddha lands, open a hundred doors of Dharma, display a hundred different bodies, and endow each with a retinue of a hundred conqueror sons.

As you progress through the grounds, these qualities grow exponentially — hundreds on the first ground, thousands on the second, a hundred thousand on the third, a thousand million on the fourth, all the way to a hundred thousand trillion on the seventh. Your ability to play the long game across lifetimes becomes extraordinary.

At the tenth ground, all your emanations become Buddhas. The point of this is to rejoice in it and start to imagine it. One way to bring the paths alive is through self-generation practice at each level — imagining what it would be like to have spontaneous bodhichitta, or tranquil abiding on emptiness where everything feels like the magical play of the mind.

commentary.title: The 'Useless Buddha' and Karmic Connections
content: In Atisha's life story, Tara tells him he can become enlightened right now through tantric practice, but it would be more beneficial to become ordained and become a teacher. Geshe-la's commentary explains that Atisha needed karmic connections with people, or else he'd be a 'useless Buddha' — all these spiritual qualities but no links to anyone.

The practical takeaway: as we gain abilities, we need to be connected to people. We want to have links, reach out to people, so we can help more and more as we grow. This applies in daily life right now — not just on the tenth ground.

commentary.title: Emanations Are Everywhere
content: If countless holy beings have emanations and we have connections to at least some of them, then there are emanations kicking around in our lives. They might appear as our house, our dog, our job — or as more surprising things. Emanations don't have an inherent history, but nothing has an inherent history. They appear with a history, just an appearance.

When we start to look for emanations, they appear everywhere. An intoxicated man screaming and dancing outside the temple window at 10 a.m. could function as a teaching: this is what the craving mind looks like. When the same man reappeared across Brooklyn later that evening, it reinforced the point — we should be suspicious of the appearances in our life. They could be emanations helping us.

commentary.title: Our Relationship to Teachings We Don't Understand
content: When we encounter teachings like grounds and paths that we don't fully understand, our reaction is worth examining. It might be wonder and inspiration. It might be total boredom — not connecting at all. It might be confusion that makes us feel bad, which can turn into anger and frustration. Or it might be intellectual dismissal — what's the purpose of this?

Confusion is actually useful. It means the mind is encountering something it doesn't understand. If we only encounter what we already understand and don't endure the discomfort of confusion, we will never grow. Being confused is an improvement over not knowing about it at all. And intelligence is not virtue — it's neutral, like height or good vision. The virtues depend on our wisdom, our spiritual intelligence, which is to be developed.

dataShares.speaker: Fran
dataShares.summary: Practiced rejoicing in the virtues of others and herself — while lying down. Reflected that if we rejoice in the mind of bodhichitta, there's no way it won't be pure.

dataShares.speaker: Alexis
dataShares.summary: Prefers the word 'jubilate' rather than 'rejoice' — it captures the energy better. Also reflected on the importance of paying attention to people around us, seeing them rather than walking past them as scenery. Noticed that KK's story about the man outside the window only worked because he actually saw him the first time.

dataShares.speaker: Jose
dataShares.summary: Purified his dissatisfaction with not feeling satisfied with food by recognizing it as the result of withholding from others in the past. Found that putting in the time to really make the regret work is the biggest factor in whether purification succeeds.
